transparent.business_two_sentences: Sarepta Therapeutics, Inc. is a commercial-stage biopharmaceutical company that sells two FDA-approved exon-skipping drugs for genetically defined subsets of Duchenne muscular dystrophy and develops an investigational one-time gene therapy for the disease. Roche holds an exclusive ex-U.S. license to the gene-therapy candidate under a December 2019 collaboration agreement, while Sarepta retains all U.S. rights [c16][c18].

claims.text: Study 102 was a randomized 1:1, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 41 ambulatory boys ages 4-7 with genetically confirmed Duchenne muscular dystrophy (20 treated, 21 placebo).
The gene therapy met its primary biological endpoint: mean micro-dystrophin expression of 28.1% by western blot at 12 weeks (p<0.0001).

The primary functional endpoint (48-week NSAA motor-function score) was not statistically significant between groups (p=0.37): treated patients improved 1.7 points from baseline (within-group p=0.009) versus 0.9 points for placebo (within-group p=0.1411).
In the pre-specified 4-5 year-old age subgroup (n=16), treated patients showed a statistically significant 4.3-point NSAA improvement versus 1.9 points for placebo (p=0.0172).
Secondary biological endpoints (vector genome copies, percent positive muscle fibers, staining intensity) were all reported as met.

No new safety signals were identified; about 85% of the treated group had a treatment-related adverse event versus 43% of placebo; four serious treatment-related adverse events occurred (three in the treated group, including rhabdomyolysis and transaminase elevation, one in placebo).

Management said an imbalance between treatment arms may have contributed to the missed functional result, and a follow-on trial using the company's planned commercial manufacturing process has begun enrolling, with biomarker and safety results expected in the second quarter of 2021.
The Study 102 topline results were published January 7, 2021 at 4:05 PM Eastern time, after the regular trading session closed.

Study 101 was an open-label, uncontrolled study of four ambulatory boys ages 4-7 who each received a single infusion of the same gene therapy at a stated dose of 2x10^14 vector genomes per kilogram; at two years post-infusion, participants showed a mean 7.0-point improvement on the NSAA motor-function score versus baseline, with no placebo comparator.

In Study 101, mean micro-dystrophin expression at 12 weeks was 81.2% of muscle fibers positive by immunohistochemistry (96% mean staining intensity) and 95.8% by western blot; the therapy was described as well tolerated over two years, with all adverse events mild or moderate and occurring within 90 days of treatment, and no serious adverse events.
Third-quarter 2020 product revenue was $121.4 million, up about 23% from the third quarter of 2019.
Cash, cash equivalents and investments were approximately $1.8 billion as of September 30, 2020, compared to approximately $1.1 billion as of December 31, 2019.
Third-quarter 2020 R&D expense was $190.4 million (nine-month 2020 R&D was $515.1 million); third-quarter 2020 SG&A expense was $75.4 million (nine-month 2020 SG&A was $231.8 million).

On August 25, 2020 the FDA accepted, under priority review, the NDA for a third exon-skipping drug candidate addressing about 8% of Duchenne muscular dystrophy patients, with a regulatory decision date of February 25, 2021; the NDA had been submitted in June 2020.

The Phase 3 trial supporting that application (the ESSENCE study) was a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-center study using weekly intravenous infusions for up to 96 weeks plus an open-label extension, assessed via six-minute walk testing and muscle biopsy; an interim analysis showed a statistically significant increase in dystrophin protein production versus both baseline and placebo, though the specific percentage and p-value were not disclosed in this release.

Full-year 2019 revenue was $380.8 million, almost entirely from the company's first approved exon-skipping drug (about 13% of Duchenne muscular dystrophy patients addressable), since the second approved drug (up to about 8% of patients addressable) launched only in mid-December 2019 and its 2019 revenue was described by the company as immaterial.

As of September 30, 2020: cash and cash equivalents were $1,474.6 million, short-term investments were $341.5 million, long-term debt was $700.5 million, and shares outstanding were 78,913,045 (as of October 30, 2020).

The company is a commercial-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on RNA-targeted and gene therapies for rare diseases; its two approved drugs use a chemistry that causes the body to skip a specific faulty exon of the dystrophin gene, while its investigational gene therapy instead delivers a shortened, functional dystrophin gene directly to muscle cells via a viral vector designed for systemic delivery.

Under a December 2019 collaboration and license agreement, a large multinational pharmaceutical partner (Roche) paid an upfront amount of $1.15 billion (comprising $750 million in cash and $400 million via a purchase of 2,522,227 Sarepta shares at $158.59 per share) for an exclusive license to develop and commercialize the gene therapy outside the United States, with up to $1.73 billion in additional milestone payments, royalties described as 'mid-teens' on net sales outside the U.S., and shared global development costs; Sarepta retained all U.S. rights.
Third-quarter 2020 operating margin was about -95.2% (operating loss of $137.1 million divided by total revenue of $143.9 million); the comparable third-quarter 2019 margin was about -124.8%.

Standalone third-quarter 2020 operating cash flow was approximately -$238.2 million (nine-month year-to-date operating cash flow of $282.0 million minus six-month year-to-date operating cash flow of $520.2 million); the comparable standalone third quarter of 2019 was approximately -$67.4 million.
